audits.mathematicalReason: Parallelism and vertical angles give △CDE ∼ △ABE, so the requested area ratio is (CD/AB)². Let O be the circle's center and R its radius. The perpendicular diameter bisects CD, giving symmetry about the perpendicular bisector of AB. Consequently, ∠CAB = ∠ABD = β. Since ED extends EB, the exterior-angle theorem in △ABE gives α = 2β. The inscribed-angle theorem then gives ∠COB = 2β = α. Projecting OC onto the direction of AB gives CD/2 = R cos α, whereas AB = 2R. Thus the area ratio is cos² α. The nondegenerate configuration shown has 0° < α < 90°, so acute-angle trigonometry applies.

figureEvidence.fact: AB is the diameter, and CD is the lower parallel chord, with D on the left and C on the right.
AC and BD cross internally at E; the marked α is the angle between EA and ED, so ED is opposite to EB.

audits.mathematicalReason: Because 6² + 8² = 10², ∠ACB = 90°. If H is the perpendicular foot from C to AB, the triangle-area formula gives CH = (6·8)/10 = 4.8. For any circle through C tangent to AB at T, CH ≤ CT ≤ 2r, so r ≥ 2.4. The circle with diameter CH attains this bound and is tangent to AB at H. Since Q and R lie on AC and BC, ∠QCR = 90°; therefore QR is a diameter of the minimizing circle and QR = CH = 4.8. The coordinate route is also valid: place AB on y = 0 and C at (0,h). A tangent circle through C has center (u,r), and u² + (h−r)² = r² gives r = (u²+h²)/(2h), whose minimum is h/2.

figureEvidence.fact: The circle passes through C and is tangent to the sloping side AB; Q is its second intersection with AC, and R is its second intersection with BC.
QR joins those two second intersections. The right angle at C is established from the stated side lengths, not merely from the drawing.

audits.mathematicalReason: The given arc MA makes ∠MCA = 40°, hence ∠ACP = 140°. Triangle ACP therefore has ∠APC = 30°. The equal angles CAP and CBP, with A and B on the same side of CP, make A, B, C, P concyclic. Opposite angles give ∠ABP = 40°, so ∠ABC = 40°−10° = 30°. Since CA = CB, △ABC is isosceles and ∠ACB = 120°. Thus ∠BCP = 140°−120° = 20°, equal to arc BN. The sine-law alternative is also valid: writing x = ∠BCP and r = CA = CB gives CP/r = sin 10°/sin 30° = sin 10°/sin(170°−x). The nonzero sin 10° cancels, leaving sin(x+10°) = 1/2. The admissible branches are x = 20° and x = 140°; the latter would make B = A and is excluded. Only the special numerical value sin 30° = 1/2 is needed.

figureEvidence.fact: M, C, P, N are collinear in that order, with A and B on the upper semicircle and on the same side of CP.
The marked angles are ∠MCA = 40°, ∠CAP = 10°, and ∠CBP = 10°; CP and CN have the same direction.

audits.mathematicalReason: The two right-angle marks make AB and CD parallel. Using A = (0,0), B = (13,0), C = (13,4), the leftward segment CD = 3 places D at (10,4). Hence BD = √(3²+4²) = 5 and AD = √(10²+4²) = √116 = 2√29. Since 100 < 116 < 121, we have 10 < AD < 11, so 15 < AD+BD < 16. The candidate correctly combines segment subtraction, the Pythagorean theorem, and square-root comparison.

figureEvidence.fact: AB = 13, BC = 4, and CD = 3; right-angle marks occur at B and C.
D lies left of C, on the same side of the vertical BC as A, so the horizontal displacement from A to D is 13−3 = 10.

audits.mathematicalReason: Place the bottom rectangle at [−1,1]×[0,1] and the upper square at [−1/2,1/2]×[1,2]. For each reflected vertex pair, projecting a proposed center onto the symmetry axis cannot increase its maximum distance to that pair. Thus consider centers (0,t). The bottom corners and top corners require R² ≥ max{1+t², 1/4+(2−t)²}. These expressions agree at t = 13/16. For t below this value the top-corner bound is at least its value there; for t above it the bottom-corner bound is at least its value there. Therefore R² ≥ 425/256. At (0,13/16), all remaining vertices are also within this radius, and convexity of the disk ensures containment of all three squares. Hence R = 5√17/16. Independently, the supporting triangle with vertices (−1,0), (1,0), (1/2,2) is acute, has area 2 and sides 2, 5/2, √17/2, giving this circumradius by abc/(4K). Its circumcenter lies inside the triangle, so any shift of center makes some vertex farther than that circumradius, establishing minimality for that route as well.

figureEvidence.fact: The lower part consists of two unit squares side by side, and a third unit square is centered directly above them.
The figure has vertical reflection symmetry; its overall width and height are both 2, while the upper square has width 1. These determine the extreme-vertex coordinates used.

audits.mathematicalReason: The right triangle has hypotenuse AB = √(12²+5²) = 13. The arc centered at A gives AM = 12, and the arc centered at B gives BN = 5. Thus AN = AB−BN = 8. Since AN = 8 < AM = 12, the order along the hypotenuse is A, N, M, B, and MN = AM−AN = 12−8 = 4. Both assessed scopes and the circle-radius support are directly applicable.

figureEvidence.fact: AC is labeled 12 and BC is labeled 5, and M and N lie on the hypotenuse AB.
The arc from the A-centered circle meets AB at M, and the B-centered arc meets AB at N, consistent with the order A, N, M, B.

audits.mathematicalReason: Draw diagonal AC. In right △ABC, AC = √(3²+4²) = 5, and its area is 3·4/2 = 6. Triangle ACD has sides AC = 5, CD = 12, AD = 13. Since 5²+12² = 13², the converse of the Pythagorean theorem gives ∠ACD = 90°, so its area is 5·12/2 = 30. Convexity makes the diagonal an internal subdivision, so the quadrilateral's area is 6+30 = 36. The candidate's decomposition and supporting scopes are defensible.

figureEvidence.fact: The boundary order is A–B–C–D, with AB = 3, BC = 4, CD = 12, AD = 13, and a right-angle mark at B.
The displayed quadrilateral is convex, consistent with using AC to split it into two nonoverlapping triangles.

audits.mathematicalReason: Extend the two tangent lines to their intersection V. Each center is equidistant from the two sides of the same angle and therefore lies on its internal bisector. Homothety about V gives a fixed ratio k = r_i/VO_i, with 0 < k < 1. Consecutive external tangency gives VO_(i+1)−VO_i = r_i+r_(i+1), so (r_(i+1)−r_i)/k = r_i+r_(i+1). Hence r_(i+1)/r_i = (1+k)/(1−k), a constant, and the five radii form a geometric sequence. Its first, third, and fifth terms also form a geometric sequence, so r_3² = 8·18 = 144. Radii are positive, giving r_3 = 12. No particular angle between the lines or numerical common ratio is required.

figureEvidence.fact: All five circles occupy the same wedge between the nonparallel lines L1 and L2 and are tangent to both lines.
Consecutive circles are externally tangent, with radii increasing from the leftmost circle to the rightmost; the middle circle is the third of the five.
